scope: Per-build device checks. build verify runs every rule on the exported image set; each rule states why it exists. Paths are target-files member paths; kernel: paths are files of the recorded kernel run.

rules.why: Sensors work on stock and on DiamaneOS: the multi-HAL, the Qualcomm sensor listener and its policy.
The sensors HAL is declared and its daemon is labelled.
The sensor daemon (sscrpcd) and the audio DSP daemon (audioadsprpcd) have their own labels.

The vendor multi-HAL list loads only the Qualcomm sub-HAL; the dynamic-sensor (HID) sub-HAL had no hidraw access and could not serve a head tracker. The odm list adds only our tap sub-HAL (tap-check-phone-sub-hal-listed).
The dynamic-sensor sub-HAL and the head-tracker feature are not shipped.
The sensors HAL no longer lists /dev or reads the mock dynamic-sensor properties.
The source fingerprint HAL is installed.
The FP6 framework, Settings, SystemUI, tethering and Wi-Fi overlays are installed.

The panel is pinned to 60 Hz while the camera previews: the GPU-composed 4:3 preview overruns the composite deadline at a higher refresh and janks. Done with the high-refresh denylist, the only knob that caps the physical mode.
The camera preview is allocated UBWC so the display can compose it (16:9 within the 1088-line inline-rotation limit); without this every preview frame is composed on the GPU.

AudioReach user space: the source-built primary HAL, PAL, AGM, ALSA plugins and audioadsprpcd, the stock graph services, calibration and configuration, and the AOSP service and adapters; no placeholder HAL.
The AOSP audio APEX would shadow the stock HAL.

Qualcomm's closed offload effect bundle and visualizer are not shipped, so apps' equalizer, bass boost, virtualizer, reverb and visualizer parameters reach only AOSP effects. The stock HAL loads them only if the files exist.
No configuration on the paths the effects factory reads names the closed offload bundle or visualizer.

adb asks before trusting a computer.
No init trigger starts adb on debuggable builds.
Nothing turns on adb over the network: no TCP port or TLS server property in the build properties or vendor and odm init files.
GrapheneOS's USB-C port control is on. Without it a user build has no USB data: first-stage init refuses new USB connections at every boot of a non-debuggable build and only port control lifts that.

The port states reach the USB controller's data switch and the charger firmware's input suspend. ports_disabled (Off) cuts data and then suspends the input: no charging while the OS runs. charging-only_immediate cuts data, ports_enabled turns data on, and every state but Off turns the input back on, as do charger mode and shutdown, so charging when powered off, in charger mode, fastboot and recovery is unaffected. User builds start every normal boot with data and charging off, as GrapheneOS starts Pixels with the port off, until the framework applies the stored mode: at early-boot the controller is cut and, once the charger firmware is up (after waiting for the node, again at boot), the input is suspended. Debuggable builds keep the port on at boot and write 0 there. Only ports_disabled, charging-only_immediate and the user-build boot cut turn data off, and only ports_enabled turns it on. charging-only cuts no data: the kernel refuses the next connection and the current one stays.
The data switch has its own type instead of the label shared with the controller role and other USB nodes.
Only vendor_init (the port-state triggers) and ueventd, which the platform lets write all of sysfs, may write the data switch; the USB HAL may not.
The charger firmware's input suspend, which Off sets, has its own type instead of the generic sysfs label.
Only vendor_init (the port-state triggers) and ueventd, which the platform lets write all of sysfs, may write the charger input suspend.
On debuggable builds a restrictive port mode is reset at boot and the lock-triggered modes do nothing while USB debugging is on, so a test phone cannot lose ADB.
A stored Off is applied when system_server starts, so data and charging stay off after a reboot of a user build; Pixels get this from first-stage init.

While port control holds a USB data disable request (svc, a device owner), the port reports DATA_STATUS_DISABLED_FORCE, so UsbManager passes the re-enable on and the stored mode comes back; before, the HAL's status said enabled and the re-enable never arrived.
Off turns off USB data and the charger input on the FP6, while the ADSP firmware still runs Type-C and USB PD, so Settings names what Off turns off.
rules.text: Turns off USB data and charging on the USB-C port.

rules.why: Android's advanced protection USB hook stays off: port control alone decides USB data.
OEM unlocking managed by the OS, as stock.
vendor_init may set our audio, radio and SSR properties under enforcing.
Night Light, grayscale, the colour transform Extra dim would use, and tap to wake.
The poll window property is labelled and read by the telephony framework fork.
The telephony framework reads the poll window.
The vibrator HAL with real effects, its sysfs label, no RTP node for system, not in the input group.
The RTP node is not handed to system.
The vibrator HAL is not in the input group.
Our own time daemon and no Qualcomm time_daemon policy.
Time daemon policy.
Our source IMEI provisioning tool and its init rc.
The provisioning tool runs in --write mode after the phone dry-run.
imeiprovd runs without capabilities, so only the traceability partition's group lets it read the IMEIs (read-only).
The provisioning tool runs in its own narrow SELinux domain.
No wlan_mac.bin in /vendor/firmware: the kernel's own firmware path and ueventd both look there before /mnt/vendor/wlan_mac/, so a file or link there would replace the factory MAC file.
The stock HCI implementation's firmware-download tags log warnings only: at info level they print the Bluetooth address at every Bluetooth start.
imeiprovd reads the factory Bluetooth address from the traceability partition early in boot, in its own one-shot service, so the HCI implementation does not generate one.
The Bluetooth init rc copies the factory address to the property the HCI implementation reads before its generated-address fallback, as stock tctd.rc does.
Both Bluetooth address properties have their own vendor-internal types, instead of vendor_default_prop, which every vendor domain may read.
Only imeiprovd (and init, which may set any property) can set the factory Bluetooth address property.
Only imeiprovd, vendor_init (the copy trigger), init and dumpstate (which reads every property) can read the factory Bluetooth address property.
Only vendor_init (the copy trigger) and init can set the address property the HCI implementation reads.
Only the Bluetooth HAL, vendor_init, init and dumpstate can read the address property the HCI implementation reads.
imeiprovd writes the WLAN driver's factory MAC file from the traceability partition in its own one-shot service, which init waits for at post-fs, before early-boot starts the Wi-Fi processor.

ueventd looks for firmware in the factory MAC tree, so the driver's request for wlan/qca_cld/qca6750/wlan_mac.bin finds imeiprovd's file (the kernel's own firmware path does not reach it; firmware-fallback keeps the sysfs fallback on).
The factory MAC tree has its own type, which only imeiprovd may write and only ueventd may read.
The QCA6750 driver reads its MAC file only with this option, as on stock.
Only ueventd (which serves it to the driver), init and vendor_init can read the factory Wi-Fi MAC file.
Only imeiprovd, init and vendor_init can write the factory Wi-Fi MAC file.
Only imeiprovd, init and vendor_init can create the factory Wi-Fi MAC file.
On user builds netd logs warnings and errors only: its info lines log every binder call with its results, and the interface configuration calls carry the factory Wi-Fi MAC.
On user builds the supplicant logs info and up only: at debug level it logs its own address at every Wi-Fi start, the factory MAC.
On user builds hostapd logs info and up only, as the supplicant: with Wi-Fi verbose logging its debug lines carry the hotspot's and its clients' addresses.
The WLAN driver logs the peer id, not the MAC, when a peer has no receive state; as Wi-Fi starts that peer is the phone itself, so the line carried four octets of the factory MAC.
fwrelease, its init rc and the firmware release table it checks the firmware partitions against.
fwrelease runs once after boot completes, for the booted slot only, as its own user without capabilities, at idle I/O and the lowest CPU priority, and is stopped after 60 s.
Only fwrelease's group may read the 44 firmware partition nodes of both slots; owner root keeps write access for update_engine, which has no CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE. No other node is given to the group.

The 17 firmware partitions of vendor_custom_ab_block_device that fwrelease checks have their own type, so it cannot read vbmeta, dtbo, pvmfw, multiimgqti or qweslicstore; fwrelease runs in its own domain.
The firmware release property has its own type, readable outside vendor (Settings) and set only within it.
Only fwrelease (and init, which may set any property) can set the firmware release property.
Only Settings, fwrelease, init, vendor_init and dumpstate (which reads every property) can read the firmware release property; shell cannot.
Who may read the relabelled firmware partitions: the old label's readers (init, update_engine) and fwrelease. Not a neverallow: that would hit init's and recovery's platform grants.
Only update_engine can write the relabelled firmware partitions, as with the old label (fastbootd in recovery too).
Who may read the modem and Bluetooth partitions: init, update_engine and fwrelease.
Who may read the uefi and uefisecapp partitions: init, update_engine and fwrelease.
Who may read the XBL partitions and their LUNs: init, update_engine, boot control, the TEE listener (which may not open them) and fwrelease, which ueventd keeps off the LUNs.
The SoC serial number has its own type, which no vendor rule names, instead of the soc0 directory's label.
Only the platform domains whose sysfs-wide read the platform policy fixes may read the SoC serial number; no vendor service may.
ueventd makes the SoC serial number root-only, so the non-root services the platform policy lets read sysfs cannot open it.

ueventd makes the UFS storage's serial number and its LUNs' SCSI serial and identification pages root-only; their generic sysfs label is readable by the fingerprint HAL, the composer and other non-root services.
init starts the boot control HAL as its own user with CAP_SYS_RAWIO only (the UFS BSG ioctl that switches the boot LUN needs it); stock runs it as root with every capability.
regex:
^service vendor\.boot-qti /vendor/bin/hw/android\.hardware\.boot-service\.qti
    class early_hal
    user vendor_bootctl
    group vendor_bootctl
    capabilities SYS_RAWIO

rules.why: The boot control HAL has its own vendor user and group.

ueventd gives the boot control HAL's group the GPT disks of the A/B LUNs (sdb: xbl_a, sdc: xbl_b, sde: the rest), misc and the UFS BSG node; the other LUNs, userdata's among them, keep the root-only default.
The switch that turns Qualcomm's embedded USB debugger on has its own type instead of the generic sysfs label, which vold, the USB HAL and vfio_handler may write.
Only the platform's sysfs-wide writers, ueventd and vendor_init, may write the EUD switch; they act only on the reviewed ueventd and init files (eud-stays-off).
No init file writes 1 to the EUD switch and no module options turn it on (the bootconfig check also refuses eud.enable on the command line).
No init file switches the kernel's restart mode. Restarts are cold, so memory is cleared and the previous boot's kernel log is not kept (the kernel argument check refuses reboot= as well).
The stock KeyMint HAL keeps its libkeymaster_messages on odm; AOSP owns the vendor path.
No stock libkeymaster_messages on vendor.
Fairphone stock product identity, as GrapheneOS keeps Google's.
Every partition fingerprint carries the Fairphone identity.
Casefolded, project-quota shared storage (takes effect at the next wipe).
GrapheneOS's Info app is not installed.
LineageOS's Glimpse is the gallery, with its own overlay that names it the system gallery, its sysconfig files and the notices of its bundled libraries; Gallery2 stays installed for its crop screen.
Glimpse holds the system gallery role (config_systemGallery), which gives it write access to all photos and videos.

Glimpse asks for its media and wallpaper permissions and nothing more: no INTERNET, so the gallery that can change every photo and video has no network access (the network state and wake lock come from media3, the last one from AndroidX). It is not platform-signed.

Gallery2 keeps only its crop screen, the crop handler of the profile photo picker: a component override turns off its launcher entry, viewer, picker, editor and every other component, and leaves the crop screen on.

The Updater asks DiamaneOS's update server, not GrapheneOS's.
The Updater asks for the permissions of GrapheneOS's Updater at the pin and nothing more (the last one comes from AndroidX).

NetworkStack's private DNS check asks under dnscheck.diamaneos.de, and none of GrapheneOS's check hosts is left in it.

SurfaceFlinger's main and RenderEngine threads join the top-app cpuset, as on Pixels, instead of the silver-only system-background set.
The power HAL runs as system with CAP_SYS_NICE only: our init file overrides the module service, which runs as root.
WALT sched_boost changes only through fixed init triggers on the one property the power HAL may set.
The power HAL starts writing its nodes after the boot-time CPU tuning, which no longer writes the minimum frequencies it owns.
The power HAL runs in the platform power HAL domain.

The power HAL may write the relabelled GPU frequency limits and wake trigger.

No write on the generic CPU, GPU, WALT or proc labels, and no perf HAL client grants.
The thermal HAL runs as system without capabilities: our init file overrides the module service, which runs as root.
The thermal HAL, as system, can still set the next severity threshold of each zone it monitors; the nodes stay root-owned for the thermal engine.
The perf client is our stand-in: it exports the calls the stock camera and SDM extension look up.

The camera provider calls the power HAL for its time-limited camera boosts as a plain IPower client: the only vendor domain in hal_power_client, no power HAL server role and no direct rules between it and the power or power stats HAL domains.
The power HAL defines the camera launch and shot boosts the camera's hints start, and no camera streaming mode that would cap the little cores CamX runs on.
Qualcomm's perf2 daemon (a root service), its client, plugins and configuration, and the CodeLinaro power HAL are not shipped.
Nothing declares, labels or starts the perf2 service.
The device's power stats HAL, its init file and VINTF fragment (stock FP6 has no power stats HAL).
The HAL declares IPowerStats V2, the version the framework matrix of target level 8 lists.
init starts the power stats HAL as its own user, with no other group and no capabilities.

^service vendor\.power\.stats-fp6 /vendor/bin/hw/android\.hardware\.power\.stats-service\.fp6
    class hal
    user vendor_powerstats
    group vendor_powerstats
    capabilities

rules.why: The power stats HAL has its own vendor user and group.
/dev/stats, the qcom_stats sleep counter node, is readable by the power stats HAL's user only.

The power stats HAL may use /dev/stats.

Only the seven qcom_stats commands the HAL reads: not the commands the driver maps to the wrong subsystems, not DDR frequency residency, and no write.
The qcom_stats driver, which creates /dev/stats, is loaded.
Factory AOD idle brightness in every panel timing of the DTBO; no D2 at power-on (display device tree d94b9d8).
Stock key, telephony and audio properties, each set once (stock property review).

vendor_init may set those properties under the platform policy.
The data profile property has its label.
Compressed Virtual A/B (lz4) with snapuserd in the first-stage ramdisk and recovery; a property may repeat but only as true.

snapuserd in recovery and the first-stage ramdisk.
USB tethering over NCM; the kernel has no RNDIS gadget function.
Device corrections to the stock carrier data (Settings shows Android's network-type list) are installed for CarrierConfig.
Wi-Fi connects, runs the hotspot and uses Wi-Fi Direct with randomised MAC addresses, and scans with the screen off.

The NCM gadget function and compositions exist.
NCM compositions are listed.
No QSEECom AIDL proxy; nothing looked it up. qseecomd and the kernel proxy stay.
The proxy is not declared anywhere.
The proxy domain is gone.
qseecomd and the kernel qseecom proxy stay.
The kernel qseecom proxy is loaded.
Only qseecomd (tee), KeyMint, Gatekeeper and the fingerprint HAL may open the TEE node; the platform's reference HAL domains in the list cannot start (tee-node-dormant-domains).
The same domains only may read from the TEE node, also through a descriptor another process opened.
The same domains only may write to the TEE node, also through a descriptor another process opened.
The same domains only may send commands to the TEE node, also through a descriptor another process opened.

The platform policy also lets its reference DRM, CAS, Keymaster, KeyMint, Gatekeeper, AuthGraph, Secretkeeper and hwcrypto HAL domains use the TEE node. No installed file may be able to start one of them.
/dev/smcinvoke is the only node with the TEE label: the legacy QSEECom driver and its /dev/qseecom node are not shipped.
ueventd gives /dev/smcinvoke to system and the drmrpc group, mode 0660, and has no rule for a /dev/qseecom node.
The offline camera service has no client: its stock VINTF declaration is not installed, so servicemanager refuses the registration inside the camera provider.
The CamX overrides turn off camera core dumps: they keep camera state, metadata and logs in /data/vendor/camera/coredump, and writing one after a recovery can hang the camera provider.
CamX creates an empty dump folder for every dumpsys media.camera even with its core dumps off; init makes the dump directory system-owned and read-only so the camera provider cannot write there.
The camera provider is in class cameraWatchdog, which init restarts with cameraserver, so a provider left with a hung camera session does not outlive a cameraserver restart.
No manifest, matrix or provider service definition names the offline camera service.
The camera provider may not register the offline camera service.
The CHI override and libchifeature2 link the offline camera library; without it the camera provider cannot load them.
The Adreno OpenCL runtime and compiler, selected only for the camera, and the software CAC library that links the runtime stay out; CamX's GPU node and its OpenCV users run without them.
The camera provider's seccomp loader and its system call list are installed.
The stock camera provider links the seccomp loader in place of libhardware, so it cannot start without the filter.
The loader compiles the installed camera provider policy.

Official user builds (releases) load the camera provider's filter in trap mode: a call outside its list stops the provider instead of only being logged. Test builds, official userdebug ones included, may run it log-only while its system call list is collected.

The camera provider may start threads but no processes (clone3 hides its flags from the filter), open only Unix and QRTR sockets and never map memory writable and executable; it may not run programs or trace or write other processes.
The stock display colour service has no client in this build; platform apps could start it.
No init service offers the colour or post-processing interfaces, so nothing can start a server for them.
The removed colour service has no domain, executable label or service context left, so no rule lets anything run or call it.
The composer loads the colour manager (panel calibration) and dlopens libsdm-disp-vndapis itself.
UBWC-P support is compiled out of the source-built gralloc, so it does not load libubwcp: every process that maps buffers would otherwise try, and outside the vendor HALs log a denial.
Our Bluetooth service registers the stock HCI implementation; init starts it in the Bluetooth HAL domain.
init starts our service, not the stock one.
Our service has the Bluetooth HAL label.
The stock Bluetooth service and the FM, ANT, SAR, config-store and TPI libraries it linked but never registered stay out.
The Bluetooth HCI service's system call list is installed.
Our Bluetooth service compiles the installed policy and installs it as a seccomp filter before it loads the closed HCI implementation; it aborts if it cannot, so it never runs unconfined.
The Bluetooth HCI service is built in trap mode: a call outside its list stops the service instead of only being logged.

The Bluetooth HCI service may start threads but no processes (clone3 hides its flags from the filter), open only Unix sockets, send only SIGKILL with kill (the HCI implementation's restart after a controller failure) and never map memory writable and executable; it may not run programs or trace or write other processes.
No hwservice context maps the ANT, ANT HCI or Bluetooth SAR interfaces, whose libraries are gone, to the Bluetooth HAL's label; unmapped, nobody may register them.

The sysfs firmware fallback is on, as stock.

rules.why: The load lists of the module streams are installed next to modules.load.
The fingerprint HAL answers the module's factory service registration in-process; nothing labels it.
FocalFingerprintService has no policy label.
The stock touch firmware in /vendor/firmware: exact stock bytes, root 0644, vendor_firmware_file; the kernel reads it directly.
rules.label: u:object_r:vendor_firmware_file:s0

rules.why: The vendor firmware label rule exists.
ueventd also searches /vendor/firmware.
The touch module that requests the firmware is installed and loaded.
The touch module is in the load list.
The kernel firmware path lists /vendor/firmware.
No stock Qualcomm LPA ships, nor its libraries and grants: eSIM management is DiamaneOS's own LPA.
The LPA's JNI library is gone.
DiamaneOS's own eSIM manager and its privileged-permission allowlist are installed.

The eSIM manager asks for its two privileged permissions, network access for eSIM downloads and hiding other apps' overlays over its Add eSIM windows, and nothing else (no camera; the last permission comes from AndroidX), ships disabled until the user turns on eSIM support, and is not platform-signed.
The allowlist grants the eSIM manager its two privileged permissions.
The framework's eUICC transport logs every eUICC command and answer in full at verbose level (ICCIDs; during a download the matching ID, the IMEI and the EID); these tags stay at info.
Android treats physical slot 1 as the built-in eUICC; stock leaves the list empty.
Release builds make /dev/pmsg0 unwritable; debuggable builds keep the platform default.
vendor_init may change the mode of /dev/pmsg0.
The platform /dev/pmsg0 rule is unchanged.
Recovery init does not name pmsg0.
pstore/ramoops in the FP6 device tree with GrapheneOS's Pixel layout, naturally aligned; the old /soc node gone.
Boot parameters handed to user space are logged by name only, in all three prints that carried the Wi-Fi MAC.
The download-mode driver ignores the "edl" and "qcom_dload" reboot reasons and drops the regulator handling only EDL reboots used.
The USB controller takes connect and role events from UCSI through its role switch and port graph, has no extcon, and the EUD debugger node is disabled.
The Moments switch belongs to the privacy switch driver, which trusts only the GPIO level and blocks in the lower position; gpio-keys no longer has it, and nothing can disable it from sysfs.
The privacy switch driver is built with its device-tree match and its sysfs directory.
The LPASS codec driver holds the decimators muted while the privacy switch blocks the microphones.
The WCD9378 codec driver keeps the mic biases off while the privacy switch blocks the microphones.
The camera driver holds every known image sensor on its test pattern at the CCI while the privacy switch blocks the cameras.
The laser range finder (a presence sensor) does not range while the privacy switch blocks the cameras.
The CDM reach probe (CONFIG_SPECTRA_CDM_REACH_PROBE) is for test builds only: it lets root make the camera's command DMA write a chosen register.
init writes the owner's kernel floor policy once, after the persistent properties load; the kernel refuses later writes.
Only init writes the kernel floor policy; the platform also lets ueventd and vendor_init write every sysfs file.
Only system_server (and init, which may set any property) sets the kernel floor policy for the next boot.
ro.debuggable follows the variant.
User builds are not debuggable.
The open-source linux-msm tqftpserv and pd-mapper, and the linux-msm libqrtr as libqrtr_linux_msm.so, are installed in place of Qualcomm's tftp_server and pd-mapper.
Qualcomm's tftp_server, its init file and its socket library are not installed.
/vendor/bin/pd-mapper is the linux-msm build: it loads the linux-msm libqrtr_linux_msm.so, not Qualcomm's libqrtr.so or the stock QMI and JSON libraries.
/vendor/lib64/libqrtr_linux_msm.so is the linux-msm library (qlog_setup) and exports what pd-mapper imports.
Qualcomm's libqrtr.so stays, unchanged, for the stock display, VM and QTEE libraries that link it.

rules.why: No init file starts tftp_server.
Both services have their own vendor user and group.
Both services and the modem's read-write files have their own labels.
The stock tftp_server domain is gone, and neither service is granted a capability or a network socket.
Only tqftpserv is granted access to the modem's read-write TFTP files in the vendor policy.
The GNSS HAL, its IGnss implementation and location libraries, and the HAL's init and VINTF files are the CodeLinaro source builds (device gnss/gnss.mk).
None of the eight GNSS files is Qualcomm's closed stock build.

The location libraries load only libgnss and libloc_api_v02: libgps.utils holds the allowlist function and the two names, and refuses every other name, such as Qualcomm's IZat, XTRA, NTRIP, engine-hub, diagnostic, batching and geofence libraries.
Only libgps.utils, through its allowlist, calls dlopen: no other GNSS file imports dlopen or android_dlopen_ext, so none can load a library around the allowlist.
Every GNSS file is built with CFI, as Qualcomm's own builds are (device CFI_INCLUDE_PATHS).

The HAL, its IGnss implementation and the QMI LOC client, which parse the framework's requests and the modem's reports, are built with the integer overflow sanitizer (they carry its runtime), as Qualcomm's own builds are.
libloc_api_v02 has the public QMI framework's client linked in and loads none of Qualcomm's QMI libraries.
No GNSS file names a Qualcomm assistance or cloud host.
The GNSS service registers only IGnss/default and runs as gps with groups system and gps: no Qualcomm location service, radio, diagnostic or secure-processor group, no capability.
The HAL serves no socket in /dev/socket/location (it existed only for the XTRA and DGNSS daemons); only its state directory is created.
The GNSS HAL domain reaches the modem over QRTR only: no socket in /dev/socket/location, no network socket and no capability.

The hardware video codec service and its Codec2 libraries are installed with the device rc and manifest, its configuration check and seccomp loader and policy, and both codec configurations (encoders only, and with hardware decoding on); the Android 14 Codec2 framework libraries are on odm.
No stock Android 14 Codec2 framework library on vendor: AOSP owns those paths, and a vendor copy would collide or shadow.
Decoding stays in the software codecs: the codec list has no Decoders section and the target specification lists only the five hardware encoders.
The Codec2 target specification registers only the five hardware encoders: its decoder list and its optional codec list are empty (the stock file mentions optional decoders only in comments).
The Codec2 service finds the encoder-only target specification through vendor.media.target_variant; without it the library registers every codec, decoders included.
The Codec2 service may read vendor.media.target_variant; a denied read would make it fall back to registering every codec.
The Codec2 audio service and its libraries are not shipped: compressed audio is decoded in software.
ueventd gives the encoder node to group mediacodec and keeps the Iris decoder node root-only; both are owned by root, so no system-uid process gets them through the owner bits.

Hardware video decoding is off unless the owner turned it on: only persist.diamaneos.hw_video_decode=1 selects the decoder variant and opens the decoder node to the codec service, at zygote-start; otherwise the boot state and the codec list stay encoders only.
No build property turns hardware video decoding on or fixes the codec list variant: the rc chooses it at boot from the owner's choice.
With hardware video decoding on, the codec list adds only the three non-secure Qualcomm decoders: no secure (DRM) and no low-latency variant.
With hardware video decoding on, the Codec2 target specification registers the five encoders and the three non-secure decoders; the optional codec list stays empty.

The codec service loads DiamaneOS's seccomp filter and codec gate in place of libavservices_minijail: the filter does not depend on the stock binary's own policy, and the store offers only the codecs the boot allows.
The codec gate defines the two calls the service's main() makes through it: SetUpMinijail (filter) and the Codec2 HIDL store constructor (codec allowlist).
The codec service's own seccomp policy allows no process creation or execution, no socket family but AF_UNIX (no network) and no mapping that is writable and executable; other calls fail with EPERM.
The Iris codec nodes have their own SELinux type instead of video_device, which the platform also grants to system_server, surfaceflinger, mediaserver and the camera HALs.
Only the codec service may open the Iris codec nodes.
Only Settings (and init, which may set any property) sets the owner's hardware video decoding choice.
Only init and vendor_init (media/init.fp6.media.rc, once per boot) set the hardware video decoding state the codec service checks.
Both hardware video decoding properties accept only 0 and 1.
The stock Codec2 library's 256-byte GraphicBuffer allocations bind the Android 14 sized compat object, not Android 17 libui's 3376-byte one.
